column1: Isolde/s0|Did she ever tell you it was too sweet?|She suggested more water and fewer berries. I mistook that for a serving preference.|Do you measure it now?|Yes. Remembering a good batch is easier with quantities written down.

Isolde/s1|How do you pack them now?|Cloth between the bottles, a firm basket, and straps checked before leaving.|Did the customer still pay?|For the bottles that arrived intact. My packing mistake was not their purchase.
Isolde/e0|Why stop using it for drinks?|The chipped neck was awkward to clean and pour from. Flowers do not mind.|Where do you keep it?|At home. I bring my own bottles on deliveries.
Isolde/e1|How far do you deliver?|Far enough to regret carrying extra bottles on foot.|Would a smaller basket help?|With the weight, yes. It would also mean more journeys.

Isolde/w0|Do the patrols refuse to pay?|They call the drinks part of their service. I never agreed to that arrangement.|Have you asked for the money?|Yes. Asking a second time is harder when several armed men find it funny.|Do ordinary customers pay fairly?|Most do. They understand that ingredients and glass are not free.

Isolde/w1|Are soldiers paying now?|I can ask the price without the whole market watching for an argument.|Did everyone fear their visits?|Enough that conversations stopped as soon as the uniforms appeared.|What would you like the market to sound like?|People bargaining, laughing, complaining about ordinary prices. Ordinary noise.
Nazim/s0|Who taught you to maintain it?|Father showed me the joins and repairs. I wish I had asked more questions.|Do leaks happen often?|Not often, but a small loss matters when rain is scarce.
Nazim/s1|Was the traveller in danger?|He was exhausted and desperately thirsty. Bargaining could wait.|Did he thank you?|He did. I preferred that to taking something he might need later.

Nazim/e0|What do you check on the bucket?|The handle and its fastenings, then the rope. A sound bucket is no help if the rope parts.|Was the lost bucket hard to retrieve?|Hard enough that I remember to check now.
Nazim/e1|Do people wait long for water?|Sometimes. Shade makes the wait less punishing.|Do travellers share news there?|Once they have drunk and caught their breath, usually.

Nazim/h|Why did caravans trust the cisterns?|Because people maintained them between visits. Stored water does not stay useful by neglect.|Could the market survive without them?|Not at this size. Traders need to know they can replenish water.

Nazim/w0|Has an officer tried to claim the well?|They have spoken of the crown's needs as though nobody else drinks.|Would you refuse a thirsty soldier?|No. Offering a drink is different from surrendering everyone's water.|Who maintains the well?|People who depend on it. That is why we object when someone treats it as spoils.

Nazim/w1|Will everyone still share the water?|That is the intention. We must maintain the supply as carefully as we welcome people.|What if a new ruler claims it?|We will have to object together. A new banner does not fill a cistern.|What matters most now?|Keeping it sound through the dry weather. Freedom still needs maintenance.

Halima/s0|Can smells tell you an exact town?|Sometimes a cargo suggests a route. I still ask; a scent is not a map.|What did frightened travellers forget?|Simple routines, like loosening straps or putting food away. Mother noticed and gave them time.
Halima/s1|Do you make that tea now?|When I have company. I like the smell before anyone starts talking.|Would you let a tired guest stay quiet?|Certainly. The tea is not payment for a story.
Halima/e0|Does anyone come unexpectedly?|Often enough that the extra cup has justified itself.|Do you dislike drinking alone?|Not always. I simply like being ready when somebody stops by.

Halima/e1|How do you separate them?|Small sealed containers, then wrapping to protect them on the road.|Have you spoiled a meal that way?|I once made everything in a pack smell of cumin. Even breakfast.

Halima/h|What can a knot tell you?|Some traders tie a bundle in a familiar way. It is a clue, not proof.|Do you keep written records too?|Of quantities and payment, yes. Memory alone is expensive to trust.

Halima/w0|Does every checkpoint charge a levy?|Enough do that the same sack pays several times before I sell it.|Can customers tell what raised the price?|Only if I explain. They see my counter, not the checkpoints.|Could you take a cheaper route?|A longer journey uses provisions too. Avoiding one levy can cost more elsewhere.

Halima/w1|Will spices become cheaper?|Where levies caused the cost, yes. A poor harvest will still affect it.|Do customers believe your prices now?|They can at least ask me about costs I actually control.|What will you do with the difference?|Pay my suppliers fairly and keep enough to make the next journey.

Tarek/s0|How did you break your ankle?|A bad step while unloading. After that I was the cargo.|Was the camel trying to protect you?|Perhaps. It certainly disliked the hurried pulling, and so did my ankle.
Tarek/s1|Why use bells on a caravan?|They help us hear where the animals are in poor light.|Why haven't you fixed the third bell?|I have grown used to recognising it. A tidy sound might confuse me.
Tarek/e0|How does it refuse?|It plants its feet and stops pretending we agree.|What do you do then?|Check the load, the heat and the animal. Sometimes the objection is sensible.

Tarek/e1|What changes the sound?|The pace and the footing. A hard surface makes each step sharper.|Can you follow the sound in darkness?|Within reason. Bells do not replace a visible route and a careful pace.

Tarek/w0|Why did officers refuse to rest?|They valued arriving on their timetable more than the animals carrying them.|Could you lighten the loads?|I asked. A royal cargo was treated as more important than the creature beneath it.|Do you still work for patrols?|I avoid it where I can. Their urgency has cost me too much.

Tarek/w1|When is the best time to travel?|In the cooler hours, with rests suited to the animals and the route.|Will you replace the animals you lost?|When I can care for them properly. They are not spare wheels.|Does resting make the journey longer?|Sometimes. It is still quicker than losing an exhausted animal far from water.
Suhaila/s0|Why blue birds?|She likes imagining them above a cooler landscape. I like recognising her work.|Does she ask your advice?|About thread, yes. About every color, increasingly less.

Suhaila/s1|What do people talk about?|Meals, work, children, complaints about the heat. Nothing requiring a king's permission.|Do you look forward to it?|Yes. An ordinary conversation is a good end to a difficult day.

Suhaila/e0|Does she use blue in every piece?|Not every one. Often enough that I know whose threads I am finding.|Do you keep the loose threads?|Only when I forget they are in a pocket. She has made me better keepsakes.
Suhaila/e1|Do people save you a place?|Someone usually notices when I arrive. I try to do the same for others.|What if there isn't room?|We shift, or take turns. Nobody owns the shade.

Suhaila/w0|Does the levy depend on what she earns?|It depends on what the collectors demand. That is the trouble.|Can she raise her prices?|Her neighbours are paying levies too. They have little extra to spend.|Do you help her finish the work?|I can sort thread. I cannot give her back the evenings the crown takes.

Suhaila/w1|What did you talk about?|A pattern she wants to try, for once without calculating how quickly it might sell.|Will she work less now?|Enough less to rest her hands. She still enjoys weaving.|Does she want to keep the loom?|Of course. Being forced to work late never meant she hated the craft.

Idris/s0|Which son would take you sailing?|The eldest, if I trusted his confidence before his experience.|Does the youngest have his own ambition?|He will. For now, he is trying on his brothers' ideas.
Idris/s1|Can you still make a profit?|Yes. A fair margin and a returning customer suit me well.|What if a customer has very little?|We discuss what they actually need before settling on a purchase.
Idris/e0|Would you go on that voyage?|I would ask how often the orchestra rehearsed first.|Could music help a long crossing?|Certainly. So could letting the passengers sleep occasionally.
Idris/e1|What embarrasses a customer?|Being laughed at for asking what something costs.|Do you ever refuse an offer?|Of course. I can say no without making the person feel foolish.

Idris/w0|What new demands are hurting trade?|Extra charges between towns and orders nobody agreed to pay for.|Do your sons want to leave because of that?|It is part of it. I would like them to have better reasons than fear.|Can you still keep the business going?|For now. Planning ahead becomes difficult when the demands keep changing.

Idris/w1|Will you mind if they leave anyway?|I will miss them. That is different from wishing them smaller lives.|Could the business support them now?|There is a better chance. At least we can discuss it without another levy hanging over us.|Would you join them at the coast?|For a visit. Someone must still understand the accounts at home.

Rashida/s0|Was the bowl still safe to use?|It became an ornament. I would not sell damaged glass for drinking.|Could you repeat the effect?|Eventually, under controlled conditions. Another storm was not a sensible method.
Rashida/s1|Do you admire Sela's work?|Yes. We disagree about style more than skill.|What makes your glass different?|I favor lighter forms. That brings its own difficulties in shaping and cooling.

Rashida/e0|Why was clear glass difficult?|Impurities and uneven work showed immediately. Plain glass leaves nowhere to hide.|Did you keep the bowl?|For a while. Eventually I let someone else enjoy it and made another.
Rashida/e1|Can any sand become good glass?|The materials matter. A handful from the road is not a ready recipe.|How often do you start again?|Often enough to keep the failed work out of my boasts.

Rashida/w0|Does he refuse your price?|His representatives call a lower price an honor. I call it a smaller payment.|Could you refuse the order?|Refusing the crown attracts attention I would rather spend on glass.|Is the work at least interesting?|Sometimes. That does not make being underpaid more agreeable.

Rashida/w1|What would you make for that house?|Something suited to its light and its owner, not the size of a ruler's pride.|Would you accept another public commission?|If the terms were honest and the people paying could afford it.|Does ordinary work pay enough?|When customers pay the agreed price, it can.
Bilal/s0|How did she reach the roof?|A stack of things I should never have left beside the wall.|Was Ladder any better behaved?|No. The name was a warning to myself, not a prediction.

Bilal/s1|Do you often get that quiet?|Briefly. A herd rarely keeps the same sleeping hours as its keeper.|What has Patience eaten?|Cloth, leaves, and the corner of a note I foolishly put within reach.
Bilal/e0|Did you tempt her with food?|I made the ground more interesting than the roof. Food helped.|Did you block the way up afterwards?|Yes. I learn eventually, however the goats describe me.

Bilal/e1|Can you tell them apart at once?|By their faces and habits. Living with them makes the differences obvious.|Which one should I watch around lunch?|Any goat close enough to express an interest.

Bilal/w0|Do they take the young goats?|They count them as wealth before they are old enough to leave their mothers.|Can you hide a growing herd?|Not from someone determined to count it. Goats are poor conspirators.|How does that hurt next year's herd?|Taking the young leaves fewer healthy adults later. The collector counts only this season.

Bilal/w1|Why keep two young does?|They will strengthen the herd instead of leaving me dependent on the oldest animals.|Will there be enough food for them?|I have planned for that. Keeping more than I can feed would solve nothing.|Will you sell more next year?|If the herd is healthy. I would rather count properly than promise early.

Sella/s0|How did you know a fish was good?|Freshness and condition. Ugly is harmless; spoiled is another matter.|Did customers know what was in it?|Anyone who asked. A stew is no reason to hide its ingredients.

Sella/s1|Is the patched sail safe?|He checks it. I would rather lose my familiar landmark than have him keep unsafe cloth.|Do you wait at the harbor?|When he is due back. Watching does not bring the boat faster, but I go anyway.

Sella/e0|What if several people arrive late?|Then I have to admit what is left. Kindness does not multiply fish.|Do you often eat last?|Often enough. I keep myself a portion when I remember to be sensible.

Sella/e1|Does rain always trouble the boats?|Not always. Wind and conditions at sea matter more than the smell on shore.|Who is the kettle for?|Whoever comes in chilled. They usually want something warm before a conversation.

Sella/w0|Do the collectors demand the same catch in bad weather?|That is the complaint. A number on a decree does not account for a storm.|Who comes to you hungry?|Families whose share has become too small after everyone else takes theirs.|Can the fishermen simply stay ashore?|They can avoid a dangerous crossing. They cannot avoid needing to eat.

Sella/w1|Will you still feed people who are short?|When I can. A defeated king does not instantly fill every cupboard.|What would you cook for pleasure?|A good thick pot with enough fish that I need not count each serving.|Do you expect the harbor to recover quickly?|Work and repairs take time. I am glad we can discuss them without another demand from above.

Ovid/s0|Could you recognise a workshop without looking?|Some, by the rhythm. I still get surprised when somebody changes jobs.|Did sweeping teach you music?|It taught me to listen while doing something else.
Ovid/s1|Which trade was hardest to fit in?|The smiths. Every one thinks their hammer has the proper rhythm.|Will the workers hear it?|That is the idea. I expect corrections before applause.

Ovid/e0|Does the note spoil the tune?|It gives the smooth part an interruption. People seem to enjoy knowing it is coming.|Could you remove it now?|I could. Then someone would ask where the dropped hammer went.

Ovid/e1|Do you write those sounds into music?|I borrow their rhythm, not every clatter exactly.|What throws the rhythm off?|Usually someone dropping something. Real streets do not wait for the next bar.

Ovid/w0|Did they promise to pay for the music?|Yes, before the performance. Afterwards the promise belonged to an absent clerk.|Did you find the other clerk?|I found another explanation. It did not pay the rent either.|Why keep performing for them?|A royal summons is not an ordinary invitation.

Ovid/w1|Do you expect those debts to be paid?|Not all of them. Keeping a record still matters.|What would make the records useful?|Knowing what was taken and from whom, if repayment is ever discussed.|Would you accept another official order?|With clear terms and someone responsible for payment.

Jamila/s0|What did you stop carrying?|Duplicate goods nobody bought often enough to justify the weight.|How did you learn what people needed?|By keeping track of requests instead of guessing from my own pack.
Jamila/s1|Why did you accept the gloves?|She needed supplies and had little else to trade. I could afford that bargain.|Did you see her again?|No. I wish I could tell her how useful they became.

Jamila/e0|What if a spare is genuinely useful?|Keep it. I mean unnecessary duplicates, not throwing away sensible provisions.|Have you carried too much yourself?|Enough that I recognise the stops and the sore shoulders.

Jamila/e1|Do they ask about other goods?|Sometimes. Looking is allowed even when the familiar choice wins.|How do you remember regular customers?|By what they ask for and how they use it. Names follow after a few visits.

Jamila/w0|Do the checkpoints give receipts?|Sometimes. A receipt does not help when the next officer calls it someone else's charge.|Could you predict the total levies?|Not reliably. That makes setting a fair price difficult.|Can traders complain together?|We talk. Complaints travel more slowly than the officers collecting money.

Jamila/w1|What can you plan now?|The cost of goods, provisions and travel, without inventing a margin for every surprise levy.|Will you travel farther?|Perhaps, once I know the condition of the routes.|Do you miss any excitement?|I sell supplies. I do not need the accounts to be an adventure.

Nerissa/s0|Why did your aunt choose the shallows?|So I could stand up if I panicked. Confidence came a little at a time.|When did you stop needing the float?|Before I admitted it. I had become rather attached to looking prepared.

Nerissa/s1|How does the tide affect payment?|Boats return when the water allows. Customers cannot spend a catch they have not landed.|Did the marks help your business?|They reminded me when to expect people, and when a delay might be ordinary.

Nerissa/e0|Did you lose the whole ledger?|Enough pages to learn that drying paper does not restore washed-out ink.|Do you keep copies now?|Of important figures. I also keep paper away from splashing water.

Nerissa/e1|Does the tide ever surprise you?|Weather can change what an ordinary tide does. Watching remains useful.|What do you watch for?|The waterline and the current, especially when boats are coming in.

Nerissa/h|Did your aunt mean to stay?|At first she meant to earn enough for the next step. Then the next step became a home.|What brought other settlers here?|Work on boats, trade, family. Not everyone arrived for the same reason.

Nerissa/w0|Does he tax a poor catch too?|A smaller catch still has hands reaching for it before the household eats.|Who pays when a boat is damaged?|The people depending on it. The crown does not share that loss.|Do the taxes help maintain the harbor?|Not enough to match what they take from it.

Nerissa/w1|What needs repairing first?|The working parts of the harbor that keep people and cargo safe.|Could you celebrate after the repairs?|Gladly. I would enjoy a celebration that did not leave the next morning's work more dangerous.|Who should decide how the money is spent?|The people using and maintaining the harbor should have a say.
Astrid/s0|Were Runa's gloves homemade?|Warm, thick, and plainly made. Exactly what the weather required.|Did you keep the pretty gloves too?|Yes, for weather that did not intend to punish me.

Astrid/s1|How do you know who is missing?|I learn people's habits. A saved portion is easier than assuming they already ate.|What if someone is delayed by weather?|Then a warm meal matters all the more when they arrive.

Astrid/e0|Does that happen often?|Often enough in winter. A cold traveller should not have to make a formal request.|Why keep the spoon ready?|So serving a bowl takes one less search while someone is shivering.

Astrid/e1|Does snow really muffle a knock?|A heavy snowfall quiets the street. I pay attention rather than assuming no visitor would come.|What if you miss it?|I cannot hear everything. That is why I check when I expect someone.

Astrid/w0|Do neighbours share their stores?|When they can. We know a blocked road may keep supplies away for days.|Does the crown help in winter?|Its demands arrive more reliably than its help.|What worries you most?|A long cold spell after people have already given up too much of their food.

Astrid/w1|Are the stores enough?|I keep checking. Hope is welcome, but it does not tell me how many meals remain.|Will you put more aside now?|When supplies allow. Keeping the crown's share should help.|What would make winter easier?|Sound homes, stocked cupboards, and neighbours noticing when someone needs help.
Colm/s0|What made you notice?|I could describe a week's work but not one supper. That seemed a poor bargain.|Does taking a break delay your work?|A little. Working hungry and tired delayed it too.

Colm/s1|Does Bess know when you want company?|I tell her. Expecting her to guess every evening would be unfair.|Do you prefer an empty tavern?|No. I like other people being there without having to entertain them.
Colm/e0|What meal made you slow down?|One I had paid for and barely tasted. I decided not to waste the next one.|Do you cook too?|Enough to appreciate when someone has done it better.
Colm/e1|Can talking be tiring?|When every pause feels like a mistake to fix, yes.|How do you know someone wants quiet?|Ask, then believe the answer. It need not become a puzzle.

Colm/w0|What do the proclamations ask you to give up?|Food, wages, time. Always something the speaker seems to have plenty of.|Do people believe them?|Some do. Some are simply too tired to argue in public.|Have you ever complained openly?|Carefully. Hunger gives you complaints; it does not make the consequences disappear.

Colm/w1|Do you still worry someone is listening?|Sometimes, before I remember I may finish the sentence.|What will you complain about first?|The ordinary things. Cold supper would be a refreshing subject.|Will people speak more freely now?|I hope so. It takes practice after years of watching the door.

Tessa/s0|Why did the child like the mistake?|It sounded unexpected. I worked it into the tune deliberately afterwards.|Were you nervous playing in public?|Very. The fountain seemed a forgiving audience until people gathered.

Tessa/s1|Do you know every requested song?|No. I ask them to hum it; sometimes I know it under another name.|Do sad songs spoil the mood?|Not if people want them. A room can enjoy remembering something sad.
Tessa/e0|Do you get nervous before starting?|Yes. A steady breath helps me begin at the pace I intended.|What if the room keeps talking?|I begin when I can be heard. I am a musician, not a bell.

Tessa/e1|Wouldn't a louder phrase reach them better?|They need clear music, not constant loudness. I make sure I can be heard before playing softly.|Do you watch the audience while playing?|Enough to know whether I have lost them, or whether they are simply listening.

Tessa/w0|Would guards recognise the tune?|Some might. I choose my audience carefully.|Why forbid a song?|Because people remember more than its melody. Halvard dislikes memories he did not approve.|Does playing without words feel enough?|No. It is what I can do without making every listener take the same risk.

Tessa/w1|Will people remember all the verses?|Some will. We can compare them instead of pretending one singer knows everything.|Will you perform them publicly?|When people want to hear them, yes.|What if the old words are unkind?|Then we can discuss them openly. Keeping a song does not require praising every line.

Rowan the Hunter/s0|Did he ever lose your trail?|When I had no food, he was more willing to consider other business.|Could you train him without sausages?|Yes. The sausages simply made his enthusiasm impossible to mistake.

Rowan the Hunter/s1|How do you judge what a herd can spare?|Its size, condition and young. Some days the right decision is taking nothing.|What if you need food urgently?|That makes the choice harder. It does not make an overhunted wood recover faster.
Rowan the Hunter/e0|How do you know he took it?|Crumbs and an unusually careful distance from the empty plate.|Does he try that face on Ada?|He tries it on everyone. Ada is rarely persuaded.

Rowan the Hunter/e1|What do feeding signs tell you?|Which animals use the clearing and whether there is enough food for them.|Would you leave an overused clearing alone?|Yes. It needs time, not another hungry visitor with a bow.

Rowan the Hunter/w0|Do the boundaries protect the animals?|Some limits would. A boundary keeping poor people out while royal parties hunt freely does not.|Have patrols stopped you?|Enough that I choose my route home carefully.|Do you hunt beyond what you need?|No. The crown's greed is no excuse for mine.

Rowan the Hunter/w1|Who should set the hunting limits?|People who know the land, with families who depend on it heard too.|Will you still leave some herds alone?|Yes. Their condition has not changed just because the king is gone.|Could everyone hunt freely now?|Without care, that would leave everyone hungry later.

Sverre/s0|How did you find the shed?|I had passed it earlier. I followed the fence back instead of wandering into the whiteout.|Why wait until morning?|I had shelter from the wind, but could not see the path. Leaving would have thrown away the safety I had found.

Sverre/s1|Why keep different sizes?|Children and grown travellers both arrived cold. One large pair did not suit everyone.|Did people return them?|Most did. Mother cared more that their hands warmed up.
Sverre/e0|How did she keep them dry?|She dried returned pairs before putting them back by the door.|Did she make them herself?|Some. Others came from neighbours with an unmatched mitten to spare.

Sverre/e1|Can you tell when a roof is struggling?|Sagging and new creaks need attention. I ask someone who knows the structure to check it.|Do you climb up to clear it?|Not onto a roof I suspect is unsafe. Snow is not worth falling through the house for.

Sverre/h|Could the lamps be seen in a blizzard?|Not far. They helped anyone close enough to make out a window.|Did neighbours take turns checking people?|When it was safe to go out. We paid particular attention to anyone living alone.

Sverre/w0|Did papers delay someone in a storm?|Yes. An officer wanted a name recorded while the traveller needed somewhere warm.|What did you do?|Brought the person indoors first. The questions could follow us.|Why insist on papers then?|Because the officer had an order and refused to consider the weather.

Sverre/w1|Which repairs matter most?|The stretches people depend on for supplies and reaching their neighbours.|Who will organise the work?|People who know the damage and can judge how to repair it safely.|Will everyone be able to help?|In different ways. Food and planning matter as well as lifting stones.
Runa/s0|Why did you think jam belonged in soup?|I liked both. I had not considered whether they liked each other.|Did she let you try again?|Yes, with ingredients we had discussed first.

Runa/s1|What do you enjoy about the thaw?|The change in the air, and seeing paths emerge from snow.|Do you mind the mud?|On my boots, yes. I still prefer it to wondering whether winter will last forever.

Runa/e0|Can you tell which seasoning is missing?|Sometimes. Astrid asks me to describe the taste before naming anything.|Do you like cooking yourself?|Yes. I am learning that tasting is only one part of it.
Runa/e1|Do you wear different boots after thaw?|The ones I am least upset about cleaning.|What happens when the puddles freeze again?|Then I stop treating them as harmless water and watch my footing.

Runa/h|Where do you keep the thaw water?|In containers for the gardens, where people can use it when the soil needs it.|Is it drinking water?|Not simply because it came from snow. The water we save this way is for plants.

Runa/w0|Who checks the door before speaking?|People who have something unkind to say about the crown.|Have you asked what life was like before him?|Yes. Some answers begin with another look at the door.|What would you like to talk about freely?|Why things are done the way they are, without being told the question is dangerous.

Runa/w1|What questions are you asking?|Who makes decisions now, and how the rest of us get heard.|Are people giving clear answers?|Not always. At least uncertainty no longer ends the conversation.|Does the change feel real yet?|In little moments. Finishing a question is one of them.

Eira/s0|Did the recipe give any measurements?|Very few. I keep notes so the next person has more help than I did.|Can you repair the leaning press?|It is braced for use. I check it before a batch instead of trusting the familiar lean.

Eira/s1|Where do you keep the bottles?|Stored at home, out of the light. They are samples, not things I carry everywhere.|Do you compare different years?|Yes. Notes about the fruit and weather help explain what changed.

Eira/e0|Do you keep the bad cider itself?|Not indefinitely. I keep the notes; spoiled drink is no useful collection.|What mistake taught you most?|Changing several things at once. Then I could not tell which change had caused the trouble.

Eira/e1|Does a wet year always make worse cider?|No. Different fruit may need a different balance in the recipe.|Do you adjust the sweetness?|After tasting the fruit. Last year's amounts are a starting point.

Eira/w0|Do the collectors take a fixed amount?|They arrive with a demand, whether the harvest was generous or not.|Can you explain the shortage to customers?|I do. They are tired of paying for the crown in so many ways.|What happens if you refuse?|The complaint returns wearing armor. That discourages an honest argument.

Eira/w1|Who helped with the apples?|Neighbours who picked, carried and sorted them. Making cider takes more than my recipe.|Will you celebrate with them?|That is what the barrel is for, when they can gather.|Did the crown usually take the first share?|Enough of it that thanking my helpers came after satisfying a collector.

Fenton/s0|How did you lose both boots?|I stepped into soft ground and pulled free in a hurry. The mud kept what it wanted.|Weren't you cold without the coat?|Later, yes. At the time I needed to walk more than I needed another layer.

Fenton/s1|Had you been apart long?|Long enough that hearing her voice felt more remarkable than the journey.|Did you tell her about the mountains?|After supper. She wanted to know whether I had eaten first.

Fenton/e0|Why change the ending?|A close escape was exciting. Someone expecting me home mattered longer.|Do listeners prefer the dangerous part?|Some do. They can survive a few sentences about a decent meal.

Fenton/e1|Would you rather they asked?|Depends on the memory. I appreciate being allowed to say I would rather leave it.|Have you left things out of your tales?|Certainly. A journey contains more than anyone owes a roomful of listeners.

Fenton/w0|How do you ask strangers for help?|Plainly, without reaching for my belongings too quickly. People have reasons to be cautious.|Have you been refused shelter?|Yes. Sometimes there was no room; sometimes fear had taken it.|Does travelling make you trust people less?|It has taught me both caution and gratitude. I would not discard either.

Fenton/w1|Why might trust take time?|People remember what followed the last unexpected knock.|Will you keep travelling?|I expect so. I would like the next journey to feel less like an apology.|What can a traveller do to help?|Respect a refusal, explain what they need, and pay fairly when they can.

Tallis/s0|Why not practise somewhere quiet?|I did that too. This was a lesson in keeping my place when the world interrupted.|Did the smith enjoy the music?|Eventually. At first he asked whether my teacher disliked him.

Tallis/s1|Have you asked the glassworkers?|Yes. Their suggestions include words unsuitable for half my audiences.|Why did you think they were delicate?|I confused the finished glass with the people making it. They corrected me.

Tallis/e0|What do the hands tell you?|When someone is ready to begin, and whether I need to give them another moment.|Do you signal the first beat?|A small movement, enough for us both to start together.

Tallis/e1|Do workers actually sing at the forge?|Only when the work allows it. Nobody needs a song over a warning.|How do you choose the pace?|From the task. I change the tune if it makes anyone rush.

Tallis/w0|Who gets left out of the songs?|The workers, the families, anyone whose part does not flatter the ruler.|Can you sing different verses?|With a suitable audience. I do not make strangers share a risk they did not choose.|Do people notice the omissions?|Those who did the work certainly do.

Tallis/w1|Will your song mention the people who helped?|It should. A victory account that forgets them is incomplete.|Do people want to hear about the cost?|Some do. Others need a little time before hearing losses made into a song.|Will you ask before using someone's story?|Yes, when it is their grief I would be putting before an audience.

Kip/s0|Was it really a captain's button?|Just a common design. I supplied the captain from my imagination.|Did finding the laundress disappoint you?|Briefly. Then I remembered I still liked the ship on it.
